toady

/TOH-dee/ - rhymes with roadie · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Toady means a person who flatters others to win favor.

Coach kept one toady on the bench who applauded every decision, including the ones that lost games.

Example

Every celebrity entourage has its toady: the friend who declares each rough demo a masterpiece, laughs before the joke lands, and has never once said the word 'no.'

A toady is defined by direction and motive: the flattery aims upward, at whoever holds power, and it wants something — favor, promotion, protection. That calculating angle separates the toady from someone who is merely warm or admiring.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

bootlicker: Bootlicker is blunt slang for someone who grovels before a superior, flattering shamelessly to stay in favor. It is what you call a toady when contempt wins out over description — the same upward-aimed praise, named at its most servile.

yes-man: A yes-man agrees with the boss automatically — his tool is agreement, not praise. A toady works with flattery: compliments aimed upward at whoever holds power, with a favor in mind. Both want the same protection; the yes-man nods along, while the toady applauds.

sycophant: Sycophant is the formal, written-register word for what a toady is in office talk and gossip: someone who flatters the powerful to win favor for himself. The meaning barely shifts; the setting does. A columnist writes 'sycophant'; teammates mutter 'toady.'

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

critic: someone who points out faults honestly

skeptic: someone who questions claims rather than applauding them

Where it sits · how deep the groveling goes

flatterer → toady → lackey

flatterer vs. toady: A flatterer lays the praise on thick but may want nothing more than to be liked; a flatterer stops short of the toady, whose praise is an investment aimed at power.

lackey vs. toady: Lackey goes further than toady: the toady flatters and agrees, while the lackey has surrendered entirely, running errands at a snap of the fingers.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — toad: the squat amphibian (Old English tadige)

Suffix — -y: noun-forming: a person connected with

Put it together: Toady is short for toad-eater. Traveling quack shows kept an assistant who would publicly swallow a toad — believed poisonous — so the 'healer' could cure him on the spot; the toad-eater would do anything, however degrading, for his master. Note that the -y here builds a person-noun, not this unit's title sense of 'characterized by.'

Why there's no relative to spot: The root is just toad, the animal — no other English word grows from it. What matters is the story: toad-eater shrank to toady, and the servility of that original job stuck to the word permanently.

Strength Check

Word Choice

informal / contemptuous

Toady is casual and always insulting — office talk, sports talk, gossip. It pairs off against this unit's laudatory: laudatory praise can be earned and sincere, while a toady's praise is a transaction. In formal writing, 'sycophant' fills the same slot — a word worth knowing on test day too.
